rows.en: The first traces of interpretations that have these characteristics are found in the Holy Scriptures that were written in the days of Ezra. A clear trace of this matter shines out from the things that Ezra himself relates.{v1_04_05:1} After he has told, in the book called by his name, the events⚠1 of his journey with those who went up, he relates further that the princes approached him, saying: "The people of Israel, and the priests and the Levites, have not separated themselves from the peoples of the lands, according to their abominations, of the Canaanites, the Hittites, the Perizzites, the Jebusites, the Ammonites, the Moabites, the Egyptians and the Amorites; for they have taken of their daughters for themselves and for their sons" (Ezra 9:1–2). In these words we see explicitly that what the Torah warned concerning intermarriage with the nations does not mean particular nations, namely the seven nations written in the Torah, but all the nations in general that act according to the abominations of the seven nations. So, without doubt, was the statute of the Torah that warns against intermarriage understood, and so was it interpreted at that time; for this is why they stated precisely that they had trespassed by not separating themselves from the peoples of the lands that act according to the abominations of the Canaanite, the Hittite and all the other nations against marriage with whom the Torah warned explicitly. It is an error on the part of those who say that Ezra made a new decree forbidding intermarriage with the other nations, and that it was not forbidden by the Torah.{v1_04_05:2} For if there had been no prohibition beforehand, for what reason did the princes complain against the people who had not separated themselves from the peoples of the lands? Had they not done nothing against the law? But the truth is that from of old the statute of the Torah was interpreted in this way: all the nations that act according to the abominations of the Canaanites are included in the prohibition, and the Torah spoke only of what was common. One document that was taken up into the book of Nehemiah, and whose author was without doubt Nehemiah himself, is full of religious and legal matters, and it gives us clear hints of the character of the interpretation of the Torah at that time. This document is the document of the making of the covenant, in which they made a sure covenant and wrote it, and to the sealing were the princes, the Levites, the priests and the rest of the people, who took upon themselves with a curse and with an oath to walk in the Torah of the Lord (Nehemiah 10:1–40). The later generations already held this document to be a book by itself, and in the course of time various wondrous aggadot were attached to it, which is a sign of how greatly it was prized in the nation, and also of its age (Ruth Rabbah 4). Now in this document come details of commandments and statutes, and from their description we recognize how they were understood by them and how they interpreted the words of the Torah with regard to these statutes and commandments.{v1_04_05:3} One of the statutes that they took upon themselves with a curse and with an oath is: to sanctify the Sabbath day. And it is said in particular that they took upon themselves not to take from the peoples of the land who bring wares and any grain on the Sabbath day to sell. And if we ask: was this act forbidden to them from the days of old, or did they decree it at that assembly? We find the answer in the words of Nehemiah himself, who said to those who bought wares on the Sabbath day: "What evil thing is this that you do, and profane the Sabbath day! Did not your fathers do thus, and were punished!" (Nehemiah 13:16–18). If this prohibition had not existed since long ago, how could he contend with them over it, and call this act "an evil thing," and say that their fathers too were punished for doing this evil thing? Therefore it is clear that this was not a new decree but a fixed statute from the days of old, whose traces are seen already in the words of the former prophets (Amos 8:8)⚠2 and of the latter ones (Isaiah 55:13)⚠3; and as in former times, so now too they understood the statute of the Torah thus: that to sanctify the Sabbath day the Israelite should restrain himself from doing his weekday business, even if it is not servile work.{v1_04_06:1} They further took upon themselves to bring the firstborn of their sons and of their cattle, as it is written in the Torah, and the firstborn of their herds and their flocks. Here we have before us three kinds of firstborn: the firstborn of man, the firstborn of cattle, and the firstborn of their flocks and herds. Yet he does not speak of the firstling of an ass, and instead he repeats the firstborn of cattle, which is very strange. This can only be because it is clear that in saying "the firstborn of cattle" he includes in this all kinds of cattle, even the unclean, or the unclean in particular; and in saying "as it is written in the Torah" he meant its saying (Numbers 18:15): "but the firstborn of man you shall surely redeem, and the firstling of unclean beasts." And he understood that "unclean beast" here includes every unclean beast, and that where it says elsewhere (Exodus 13:13), "and every firstling of an ass you shall redeem with a lamb," Scripture spoke only of what was common, since that was the kind of beast they had in their homes for their use, while other unclean beasts they did not raise in their homes because they were forbidden. And since Ezra and Nehemiah understood the statute of the Torah in this way, he rightly said in general terms "the firstborn of our cattle," for in truth, according to their understanding of the Torah, all beasts are subject to the law of the firstborn. Indeed, at a later time they departed from this sense (Bekhorot 5b) for a reason unknown to us; but it is clear that in Ezra's generation the statute was understood in the way we have said. The commandment of the tithe of the tithe too has a special character there. For in speaking of this commandment there is not even one word hinting that the tithe of the tithe shall be for the priest himself and for his needs. Rather he says (Nehemiah 10:38): "and the tithes of our ground to the Levites; and the Levites shall take the tithes in all the cities of our tillage. And the priest the son of Aaron shall be with the Levites when the Levites take tithes, and the Levites shall bring up the tithe of the tithes to the house of our God, to the chambers, into the treasure house." From all this it appears that the tithe of the ground is to be for the Levites, as it is written in the Torah (Numbers 18:11)⚠4, and from the tithe that is given to the Levites the Levites shall tithe their tithe; but this tithing is to be under the supervision of the priest, the son of Aaron. And after they have done this with exactness and precision and have set apart the tithe of the tithe, then the Levites shall bring up this tithe of the tithe, set apart under the priest's supervision, to the Temple, to the treasure house, and it is designated for the needs of the Temple. In their time this was very necessary, as is said there explicitly: "and we will not forsake the house of our God." And another prophet had already remarked on this (Malachi 3:10), saying: "Bring the whole tithe into the treasure house, that there may be food in my house." Now even if it be, as some of the sages of the Talmud hold, that they took this commandment upon themselves of their own accord, at any rate there is no reason to think that they took it upon themselves in another manner than that in which their fathers had been commanded concerning it by the Torah. And now, as we see that they enacted and fixed that the tithe of the tithe shall go to the treasure house and be designated for the needs of the Temple, without doubt this commandment of the Torah was understood by them in this way too. And when the Torah commanded the Levites, saying: "Thus you also shall set apart an offering to the Lord of all your tithes ... and you shall give of it the Lord's offering to Aaron the priest" [Numbers 18:28], the intention was not, in their view, that they should give the tithe of the tithe to the priest for himself and for his needs, but that they should give it for the needs of the Temple. And where it says that they shall give from the tithe the Lord's offering to Aaron the priest, it means that a tithe of the tithe shall be given to the priest and through him reach the treasury of the Temple, as they fixed in the days of Nehemiah: that the Levites shall set apart their tithe before the eyes of the priest, who shall watch over the precision and exactness of the setting apart, but the tithe thus set apart shall be brought to the treasury of the Temple.{v1_04_06:2} These few proofs give their testimony in part on the nature of the interpretations of the first Scribes and on their character. They show us that their way of understanding the Torah was a reasoned way, and that they did not go far from the plain sense of the verses. To occupy themselves with the interpretation of the Torah in this way was the holy charge they took upon themselves, for the Torah and the religion were for them the sure foundation on which to establish the happiness of the nation. To reach this aim, men of distinction, wise and God-fearing men of the generation, arose and joined together into a society that is called by the name of the Great Assembly. Over its beginning and the length of its existence a cloud still rests. The sages of both Talmuds set its beginning in the days of Ezra; only they differ in their opinions as to the number of its members: the Babylonians put their number at one hundred and twenty (Berakhot), and the Palestinians put it at eighty-five (Yerushalmi Megillah 1:5). But all agree in one opinion concerning the existence of this assembly, and that it began in the days of those who returned from the exile, and they know how to give a number for its members. And their opinion has a basis and root in the book of Ezra. For it is related there: when Ezra came up from the exile and found in the land of Judah great confusion in religious matters, and especially when he saw that they had mingled with the peoples of the lands and had married foreign women, then there were separated with Ezra men, heads of fathers' houses after their fathers' houses, and they sat down to examine the matter (Ezra 10:16). This was the first root of the Great Assembly. A few years later the assembly was completed and became a great assembly, ordered and arranged, and it enacted statutes and ordinances for its generation. This was about thirteen years after Ezra came up (A.M. 3544)⚠5, when Nehemiah came up with the king's permission, repaired the breaches of the city and rebuilt its ruins and its walls. And when they had finished the building, they met in an assembly and made a sure covenant and wrote it, and to the sealing were the princes, the priests and the Levites. All of them are designated by name, and their number, eighty-five, agrees with the number the Palestinians gave for the Great Assembly (*Moreh Nevukhei ha-Zeman*, gate 11). The opinion that this assembly began in the days of Ezra was so firm among the later sages that when they mentioned things found in the books of Ezra and Nehemiah they ascribed them to the Men of the Great Assembly (Berakhot 33b; Yerushalmi there 1:9; Genesis Rabbah 79; Ruth Rabbah 4), since in their view Ezra was the first and the head of this assembly. Since then we have become used to thinking that the Men of the Great Assembly and the Scribes are only one body under changing names. And in truth they are alike in their endeavor and in their chief charge, but for all that they were distinct in their activities. That is: the Scribes, who were called "those who give understanding," were occupied with the interpretation of the written statutes and founded laws and judgments on what followed for them from the received interpretations; it was also their task to give the people understanding and to teach it knowledge, and to make a safeguard for the Torah and to build a fence as they saw fit. The Men of the Great Assembly, however, were the members of the society that established these laws, which the Scribes derived from their interpretations, to be fixed and standing statutes in Israel in practice. Accordingly, the relation of the Scribes to the Men of the Great Assembly is like the relation of men of learning who found a religion, or who explain an old religion by the ways of learning and experience, whose activity and right is nothing but scholarly inquiry (theory), to the men who have the right of enactment and ratification, and to whom alone is given the authority to ratify and to establish the statutes that those founders and explainers taught, and by whose word alone, through their ratification and establishment, these become fixed statutes in practice. Now this matter throws light on the character of the charge that belonged to the Scribes and of that which belonged to the Men of the Great Assembly, and on how far these differed from those in their activities and their rights. For this reason it is never found that one says "an ordinance [takkanah] of the Scribes," for the right of enactment was not theirs; for the concept of takkanah denotes the fixing of a statute for a person's action, and this was not part of the Scribes' charge. Conversely, it is not found that the action of the Men of the Great Assembly is spoken of in any other term than "they enacted" [tiknu], for only they had the right of establishment and enactment. And since this is so, there is no doubt at all that the Men of the Great Assembly, being the heads of the nation, were surely the source of the rule that the Scribes were to keep in their work, and that they commanded them what the aim was that should stand before their eyes in their inquiry. This rule has been preserved for us in the Mishnah (Avot 1:2)⚠6: "Be deliberate in judgment, raise up many disciples, and make a fence for the Torah." From the character of these sayings we recognize that they are not meant for the multitude of the people, for judgment and law do not belong to the people, nor are they called upon to raise up disciples, nor is it for them to make a fence for the Torah. Rather, the Men of the Great Assembly prepared and directed these words to "those who give understanding," that is, the Scribes, to be for them a line and a measure by which to keep their charge. And they are in truth the sum of all the chief foundations for reaching the aim that the Scribes set before themselves.

rows.en: We have heard various complaints that many make against the work of Ezra: that he did not lift his soul to the sublime thoughts of the earlier prophets regarding the great and rational foundations of the Israelite religion, and that he made his first aim the founding and establishing of practical statutes. But if we consider the state of the people at that time and the level of its education, we find that these complaints are simply false. The multitude of the people, who stood at the lowest level of education, had not yet prepared their hearts to rise to the lofty thought that is the goal of the Torah and the religion. But Ezra recognized in his wisdom that the first cause of their bad religious state, and of their inability to rise from their low standing, was their lack of knowledge of the Torah. And he saw that his first duty was to make up this lack. He had no other desire but to spread Torah in Israel, so that they would know the judgment of its statutes and attain its truths. And his desire prospered in his hand, though not all at once but little by little; and from the day he began to teach statute and judgment in Israel, another spirit too was in the people, and a new light shone upon them. This light went on growing brighter for many generations. Then, as the times changed, the studies also changed and went in ways that were not imagined in the days of Ezra, as will be revealed and shown to our eyes in the coming chapters.
The work of the Scribes with regard to the Hebrew language.

The cord that binds the individuals of every nation to be of one heart and one spirit has always been religion and language. For this reason we have seen at all times that if the bond of society and unity in one of the nations has weakened a little, and its best men, its heads, its sages and its men of understanding have roused themselves to strengthen the slackened bond, then they turned their eyes first to religion and strove to renew the youth of their religion, and second they turned their eyes to the language. Those who returned from the exile also understood this, and therefore their first act was to strengthen the religion and the Torah that were an inheritance to them from their fathers; and they also gave heed to their language, which is Hebrew, which had been the language of their fathers from of old. All the days they dwelt in their land, until they were emptied from vessel to vessel [Jeremiah 48:11], Hebrew was the language they spoke. The Aramaic language they did not know and did not understand (Jeremiah 5:15). Only individuals among them, and especially the men who were close to the government, alone understood the Aramaic language (Isaiah 36:11). But from the time that people of the nations of Assyria, whom the king of Assyria settled in the cities of Israel when he exiled Israel to Assyria, mingled with them, and afterwards, at the exile of Israel from its land, when a great number went into exile to Babylon, from then on they learned the language of the people among whom they were forced to live and in whose land they were forced to dwell. When they returned from the exile, Nehemiah complained of the upheaval that had taken place in the land of Israel with regard to the loss of the language, because he found that a new generation had arisen in the Holy Land that did not know the language of its fathers and could no longer speak the Jews' language (Nehemiah 13:24). But this complaint of Nehemiah is a testimony that the knowledge of the Hebrew language had not died out entirely from among the people, since his complaint was not about all the inhabitants of the land but about individuals in it, namely the children of the mixed marriages, born of Jewish fathers who had taken foreign wives. And it also appears from this that those who returned from the exile knew the Hebrew language as before; for otherwise he would surely have had to complain about them too, as about the inhabitants of the land. And how can it enter our mind to say that they forgot it entirely during the years of their exile, when we see the sublime prophecies that were prophesied in the exile, and the psalms and songs that were sung at that time, and the books that were composed narrating chronicles and other matters? Were not all these meant to instruct the people and to teach them knowledge, and they are all written in the Hebrew language. How then shall we not say and decide that they understood the Hebrew language well? But the truth in this matter is that they spoke both languages, Hebrew and Aramaic; and indeed, as we have seen, the new generation in the land of Israel was faithless to the Hebrew language, and perhaps the young people who were born and grew up in the exile were also faithless to it and did not learn the language and the writing, so that for them too the Aramaic language was more intelligible. For this reason too it became a statute in Israel in the days of Ezra to translate the Torah into the Aramaic language. And had not the understanding of Aramaic among the multitude of the people been stronger than the understanding of Hebrew, there would have been no place for this enactment. But of all their teachings that they taught in the Aramaic language nothing is left to us of which we can say with certainty that it is from that time, except one which, by way of conjecture, may be ascribed to the first Scribes in its own writing and its own language. It is in the Mishnah, which has transmitted to us a testimony given by one of the sages who lived at the beginning of the days of the Maccabees: "Concerning the ayil kamtsa locust, that it is clean; concerning the liquids of the slaughterhouse [of the Temple], that they are clean; and that whoever touches a corpse is unclean" (Eduyot 8:4). Now this sage testified to these things, and this shows that he speaks from an ancient tradition. And the sayings to which he testified are in the Aramaic language, the like of which is not found in the Mishnah. And although we have found a few more sayings in the Aramaic language in the Mishnah, said in the name of Hillel the Babylonian, such as: "A name made great is a name destroyed; he who does not increase, decreases; he who does not learn deserves death; and he who makes use of the crown passes away" (Avot 1), these are only moral proverbs that this Babylonian was used to have on his lips. But our discussion here is about matters of interpretation and halakhot, and in this respect this testimony that Yose ben Yo'ezer gave is truly unique of its kind in the whole Mishnah. Therefore we may rightly conjecture that this is a remnant of the interpretations of the Scribes, who taught the people in Aramaic translation. However, even if the strength of the Hebrew language weakened, it was not yet broken. And it is a clear matter that from the time they returned from the land of their exile they thought to strengthen this weakness. And as they strove to raise up the Torah and to strengthen it, it being the true means to strengthen and unite their national society, so they strove to raise the standing of the language, it too being a means to reach this goal. Indeed, from all the actions that the heads of those who returned from the exile did for the good of their nation, their desire to restore all that had been forgotten to its former strength is plain to our eyes. Therefore we shall not doubt that the language did not fall behind all the other forgotten things. And it is no exaggeration if we say that in one respect the language had a further advantage in this regard. For the language is the means to the unity of the nation, because a shared language gives birth to an inclination of hearts one to another among all who speak it. Besides this, it had an advantage in that it is a pure source of the wisdom of the Torah, from which are the issues of life [Proverbs 4:23] to revive the spirit of wisdom and knowledge and the fear of the Lord among the nation, since it is the language in which their holy writings were written. There is no doubt that their longing to raise up the language had already become human action immediately after they came up from the exile. For we see how, out of his great complaint and vexation [1 Samuel 1:16], Nehemiah contends with his people because their young people speak with a stammering lip and another tongue [Isaiah 28:11] and cannot speak the Jews' language. Therefore, from this complaint of his about the lack of knowledge of the language that had grown strong among them, we can surely judge rightly that he did not rest nor keep quiet until he had made an effort to make straight what was crooked, to improve the state of the language and to restore it to its former condition. A great proof of this endeavor of theirs is given us by the enactment of the prayers, the benedictions and the praises that were enacted during the time of the first generations of the Scribes. Indeed it will not enter our mind to decide that all the prayers and benedictions ascribed to the first generations are in truth the work of their hands and their enactments, for no one who considers the matter with faithful and upright criticism can agree to this in general; but it cannot be denied either that some of the prayers and benedictions are children of the first generations. Now these prayers and benedictions were all composed in the Hebrew language, and therefore we see two things from this. First: that this language was understood by the people. And further this: that they strove to strengthen it and to raise it up. For had it not been so, how could it have entered their mind to establish the prayers and benedictions in a language that they did not understand, and that they did not wish to strengthen and keep alive? Now it is clear that the Hebrew language was only weakened in their hands, and even this weakness was only among the multitude of the people; but among the sages it did not weaken, rather they always held fast to it and strove to raise its standing. And for this reason it is not surprising that all the words of the Oral Torah, which include many sayings of the Scribes, have all reached us in the Hebrew language. But the Aramaic language, which they came to know during the days of the exile, exerted a great force on the Hebrew language, until it bred and made grow various new characteristics on the soil of the Hebrew language. These characteristics are already recognizable in all the books of this period, and of the time before and after it, in those written in plain style (prose) as in those written in poetic style. Yet it is self-evident that in this respect plain style differs from poetic style: since the character of the language of poetry is to speak in pure and choice diction, the poet guards himself carefully against all the foreign elements that spoil the beauty, and against every alien characteristic that the multitude of the people attached to the language. Therefore the corruption of Hebrew through the force of Aramaic did not harm poetic style so much; and even though in psalms and songs that are children of this time there are, here one and there one, places where the marks of Aramaic are recognizable, nevertheless, since these are few and slight, the spirit of the old Hebrew still hovers over all these remnants, and the marks of their time that cling to them did not take away their beauty and the loftiness of their diction. Not so is it in plain style. Since in it the writer makes known and sets down his thoughts in the common language that he is used to speaking, he will therefore not escape the foreign elements that were born in the language in the course of time, and sometimes he will choose them on purpose, because in the common language he will explain and state his meaning more precisely to the multitude of the people, who are used to the common language. And for this reason the language is very hard in the books of this time written in plain style, such as Ecclesiastes, Chronicles, Daniel, Ezra, Nehemiah and the Scroll of Esther, on all of which the character of the Aramaic language weighs heavily. Now at any rate we see that in all the books of this time, both the books written in plain style and those written in poetic style, the character of the Aramaic language has grown strong over them all. And likewise in the benedictions and prayers whose foundation is in that time, it is also clearly seen that the language in which they were composed was no longer of the purity of the old Hebrew language. Still more do we find a change in the character of the language in the sayings on matters of Torah and statutes that they spoke to the people and to their disciples. Because of this great change the masters of the Talmud already gave a special name to the language in which things on matters of Torah were said or written, and called it: the language of the sages. And it is the language that we call: the New Hebrew language. We do not call it new because it uses words of which no mention is found in the Holy Scriptures; for the absence of their mention in the Holy Scriptures is no proof of their non-existence. But we call it new because marks are seen in it that are faithful signs that it changed its character, since the character of Aramaic grew strong over it. And at a later time it changed its character still more, because the characteristics of other languages too, especially Greek and Latin, came into it and they too changed its character. And indeed, if we consider the matter well, we find that they were forced to this. Nor is it a new thing under the sun [Ecclesiastes 1:9]; has not necessity at all times been the mother of every new invention? These generations too were pressed by necessity to widen the language, and this widening changed its character. For the times changed, and with them the kinds of knowledge too. New opinions and new concepts spread among them, and they were forced to invent words and terms to describe them in speech, for the old Hebrew did not suffice; and they used Aramaic and Syriac after the manner of Hebrew, until they were able to speak of every new matter and concept. This is not the place to inquire into the particular characteristics that the Hebrew language had at that time; we say only in general that they did not neglect to hold fast to their language, and even if its character changed in part, this is no proof that it went backward.{v1_04_10:1}

footnotes.en: 1 Chronicles 5:1: "and because he defiled his father's couch, his birthright was given to the sons of Joseph — and the genealogy is not to be reckoned after the birthright. For Judah prevailed above his brethren, and of him came the ruler; but the birthright was Joseph's." This is an explanation of what is written in the Torah, "Reuben, you are my firstborn" etc. [Genesis 49:3], where it is not said to whom Jacob gave the birthright, and who was reckoned as firstborn, and in what respect he was reckoned as firstborn. On this the book explains that the birthright was Joseph's, and it judged so from the event before Jacob's death, when he blessed Joseph and said: "Ephraim and Manasseh, as Reuben and Simeon, shall be mine" [Genesis 48:5]; and this is why it says "to the sons of Joseph." "But not to be reckoned in genealogy after the birthright" means that the birthright was not given to him in respect of lineage and pre-eminence over all his brothers, but Judah was the one who prevailed over his brothers, and the birthright was Joseph's in respect of two tribes coming from him.

2 Samuel 24:1: "And again the anger of the Lord was kindled against Israel, and he moved David" etc. But in 1 Chronicles 22:1⚠1 he changed the words and wrote: "And Satan stood up against Israel, and moved David" etc. This change is without doubt according to the concept of his time, which believed in the existence of a particular Satan who incites man to evil; and the name Satan in this sense is not found in ancient books. See below, chapter 23⚠2. He also called the Temple by the name "house of sacrifice," and this too is according to the concept of his time; see above, chapter 3, in the note.

footnotes.en: 2 Samuel 24:3: in the mouth of Joab is put: "But why does my lord the king delight in this thing?" The reason why Joab did not agree with the king's wish is not explained there. But in Chronicles he adds the reason and says: "why should he be a cause of guilt to Israel?" [1 Chronicles 21:3]. Likewise it is not said in Samuel why David did not go to Gibeon at the time of the plague to offer sacrifices. But Chronicles says that he did not go to Gibeon because "he was terrified because of the sword of the angel of the Lord" [1 Chronicles 21:30]. Likewise, in the service of the Levites it is said that they shall serve from twenty-five years old to fifty years old (Numbers 8:24)⚠1, and elsewhere it is said from thirty years old to fifty (ibid. 4:20)⚠2; in any case they were not to be less than twenty-five years old for the service. And so it was until the days of David (1 Chronicles 23:3), but at the end of his days it was not so. The author of the book of Chronicles relates that they were counted from twenty years old, and adds the reason for the matter: for David said, "The Lord God of Israel has given rest to his people, and he dwells in Jerusalem for ever; and also the Levites shall no more carry the tabernacle" etc. (ibid. 23:24–26). By this the reason appears why David set aside the commandment of the Torah: because it was no longer needed for his time. See on this the glosses of Naḥmanides on the *Sefer ha-Mitzvot*, root 3.

footnotes.en: We have already said before this that the book of Ezra as it lies before us was composed some generations after Ezra's time. But it is clear that it contains parts that Ezra himself wrote, which the author took up into his book in their own writing and language; and one of these parts is chapters 8–9, in which Ezra speaks in the first person. Likewise in the book of Nehemiah: though it too was composed by a later author, most of its parts were nevertheless written by Nehemiah's hand, and one of them is this document of the making of the covenant. Whoever wishes to understand the matter should consult Zunz, pp. 12 to 35, and Herzfeld, vol. 1, p. 306 and following.

See Kiddushin (68b), and Maimonides, Laws of Forbidden Relations 12:1, and the *Tur*, section 44, and in the book *Mevo ha-Talmud* by R. Chajes, who decided that Ezra decreed against marriage with the other nations; and this is not correct.

In the Yerushalmi, Shevi'it 6:1 and Kiddushin 1:9 and in many places, they said that some of the commandments listed there they took upon themselves of their own accord; and for one of them the sense of the verse is also so, for it says: "And we laid upon ourselves commandments, to give the third part of a shekel yearly" [Nehemiah 10:33]. And in the Gemara they said so also of the commandment of the tithes. But even if it be as they say, that they took it upon themselves of their own accord, it is at any rate clear that they took it upon themselves with all its judgments, statutes and conditions as stated for this commandment in the Torah; or, as this commandment was understood by them, so they took it upon themselves. And they said explicitly there: "to observe and do all the commandments of the Lord our Lord" [Nehemiah 10:30], and it goes on to list what the commandments are.

It is a known and widespread matter that buying and selling on the Sabbath is forbidden by rabbinic law, as a decree lest one write; and so the codifiers wrote as a matter of course. And in Beitzah (27b): R. Judah said in the name of Samuel: one may not fix prices at the outset for a beast on a festival; and Rashi explained: for buying and selling on the Sabbath and festival is forbidden (read: Ezra forbade it) in the book of Ezra. And they said (ibid. 37a): one may not consecrate etc., a decree on account of buying and selling, which is forbidden by Scripture: "nor pursuing your business" etc. [Isaiah 58:13]; or else, one may come to writing etc.; and if you say, this is a decree upon a decree, it is all one decree. And R. Y. P.⚠1 remarked on this contradiction. Now even for Rashi it was not settled that buying and selling is forbidden by way of a decree, and according to the first explanation it is from the words of tradition. And he was forced to explain that the prohibition already existed before Ezra, as we have proved in the text from Scripture. And that he brings a proof there (27b) from Ezra is because he said that buying and selling on the Sabbath and festival is forbidden; and the festival is not mentioned in Isaiah, but is stated very plainly in Ezra⚠2, where it says: "we will not take from them on the Sabbath or on a holy day" [Nehemiah 10:32]. The main point is that this prohibition was then held to be among the prohibitions of the Torah, and is not a decree. And it is clear to me that for all the ancients buying and selling was a Torah prohibition, as we have shown from the verses. Nor do we have from the Talmud any explicit proof against this.

1.note: Abbreviation left unexpanded; perhaps R. Isaiah Pick (Berlin), glossator of the Talmud.

2.note: The verse is Nehemiah 10:32; Weiss counts Nehemiah with the book of Ezra.

footnotes.en: If we examine closely the verses in the Torah that speak of the gifts to the priests and the Levites, we find in all of them that it says explicitly and clearly to whom they shall belong as an inheritance, and it uses the words "shall be yours," "I have given them to you," "shall be yours," "I have given you," "I have given as an inheritance." These expressions are clear and leave no room for two meanings, and we know clearly to whom the gifts shall belong as an inheritance. But the verse on the matter of the tithe of the tithe is obscure, and we can interpret it in two senses. In saying "and you shall give of it the Lord's offering to Aaron the priest" [Numbers 18:28], it is possible that it meant that the giving shall be to Aaron so that it shall be his inheritance; and it is also possible to interpret that the giving shall be to the priest but it shall not be his inheritance, only that the tithe shall be given into his hand and from his hand reach the treasury of the Temple. And this second interpretation agrees with what they took upon themselves in the days of Ezra with regard to the tithe of the tithe.
